# protobuf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#library-to-read-and-write-protocol-buffers-data)Library to read and write protocol buffers data

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate has one feature, which is `with-bytes`.

`with-bytes` enables `protobuf` crate support for
[ bytes crate](https://github.com/tokio-rs/bytes):
when parsing bytes or strings from

`bytes::Bytes`,
`protobuf` will be able to reference the input instead of allocating subarrays.Note, codegen also need to be instructed to generate `Bytes` or `Chars` for
`bytes` or `string` protobuf types instead of default `Vec<u8>` or `String`,
just enabling option on this crate is not enough.

See `Customize` struct in [ protobuf-codegen crate](https://docs.rs/protobuf-codegen).

[§](https://docs.rs#accompanying-crates)Accompanying crates

- `protobuf-json-mapping`
- `protobuf-codegen`- `.proto`crates.
- `protoc-bin-vendored`- `protoc`command packed into the crate.
- `protobuf-parse`- `.proto`file parser. Rarely need to be used directly, but can be used for mechanical processing of- `.proto`files.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [descriptor](https://docs.rs/descriptor/index.html)
- Generated file from `google/protobuf/descriptor.proto`
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Utilities to support “extension” fields.
- [plugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/index.html)
- Generated file from `google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.proto`
- [reflect](https://docs.rs/reflect/index.html)
- Reflection implementation for protobuf data
- [rt](https://docs.rs/rt/index.html)
- Functions and types used by generated protobuf code
- [rustproto](https://docs.rs/rustproto/index.html)
- Generated file from `rustproto.proto`
- [text_](https://docs.rs/text_format/index.html)- format
- Protobuf “text format” implementation.
- [well_](https://docs.rs/well_known_types/index.html)- known_ - types
- Generated code for “well known types”

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chars](https://docs.rs/struct.Chars.html)
- Thin wrapper around `Bytes`which guarantees that bytes are valid UTF-8 string. Should be API-compatible to`String`.
- [Coded](https://docs.rs/struct.CodedInputStream.html)- Input - Stream
- Buffered read with handy utilities.
- [Coded](https://docs.rs/struct.CodedOutputStream.html)- Output - Stream
- Buffered write with handy utilities
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumOrUnknown.html)- OrUnknown
- Protobuf enums with possibly unknown values are preserved in this struct.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type for protobuf operations.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageField.html)- Field
- Wrapper around `Option<Box<T>>`, convenient newtype.
- [Special](https://docs.rs/struct.SpecialFields.html)- Fields
- Special fields included in each generated message.
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/struct.UnknownFields.html)- Fields
- Hold “unknown” fields in parsed message.
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/struct.UnknownFieldsIter.html)- Fields - Iter
- Iterator over `UnknownFields`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/enum.UnknownValue.html)- Value
- Unknown value.
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/enum.UnknownValueRef.html)- Value - Ref
- Reference to unknown value.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [VERSION](https://docs.rs/constant.VERSION.html)
- protobuf crate version
- [VERSION_](https://docs.rs/constant.VERSION_3_7_2.html)- 3_ - 7_ - 2
- This symbol can be referenced to assert that proper version of crate is used

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.Enum.html)
- Trait implemented by all protobuf enum types.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.EnumFull.html)- Full
- Trait is implemented for all enum types if lite runtime is not requested.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.Message.html)
- Trait which is implemented by all generated message.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.MessageDyn.html)- Dyn
- Dynamic-dispatch version of either generated message or dynamic message.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.MessageFull.html)- Full
- Trait implemented for all the generated messages, except when lite runtime is enabled.
- [Oneof](https://docs.rs/trait.Oneof.html)
- Trait implemented by all oneof types in generated code.
- [Oneof](https://docs.rs/trait.OneofFull.html)- Full
- Implemented by all oneof types when lite runtime is not enabled.

[ bytes crate](https://github.com/tokio-rs/bytes):

# bytes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytes/^1.1/

## Expand description

Provides abstractions for working with bytes.

The `bytes` crate provides an efficient byte buffer structure
([ Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)) and traits for working with buffer
implementations (

[,](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.Buf.html)

`Buf`[).](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.BufMut.html)

`BufMut`[§](https://docs.rs#bytes)`Bytes`

`Bytes` is an efficient container for storing and operating on contiguous
slices of memory. It is intended for use primarily in networking code, but
could have applications elsewhere as well.

`Bytes` values facilitate zero-copy network programming by allowing multiple
`Bytes` objects to point to the same underlying memory. This is managed by
using a reference count to track when the memory is no longer needed and can
be freed.

A `Bytes` handle can be created directly from an existing byte store (such as `&[u8]`
or `Vec<u8>`), but usually a `BytesMut` is used first and written to. For
example:

```
use bytes::{BytesMut, BufMut};
let mut buf = BytesMut::with_capacity(1024);
buf.put(&b"hello world"[..]);
buf.put_u16(1234);
let a = buf.split();
assert_eq!(a, b"hello world\x04\xD2"[..]);
buf.put(&b"goodbye world"[..]);
let b = buf.split();
assert_eq!(b, b"goodbye world"[..]);
assert_eq!(buf.capacity(), 998);
```
In the above example, only a single buffer of 1024 is allocated. The handles
`a` and `b` will share the underlying buffer and maintain indices tracking
the view into the buffer represented by the handle.

See the [struct docs](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#buf-bufmut)`Buf`, `BufMut`

These two traits provide read and write access to buffers. The underlying
storage may or may not be in contiguous memory. For example, `Bytes` is a
buffer that guarantees contiguous memory, but a [rope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rope_(data_structure)) stores the bytes in
disjoint chunks. `Buf` and `BufMut` maintain cursors tracking the current
position in the underlying byte storage. When bytes are read or written, the
cursor is advanced.

[§](https://docs.rs#relation-with-read-and-write)Relation with `Read` and `Write`

At first glance, it may seem that `Buf` and `BufMut` overlap in
functionality with [ std::io::Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html) and

[. However, they serve different purposes. A buffer is the value that is provided as an argument to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write``Read::read` and `Write::write`. `Read` and `Write` may then
perform a syscall, which has the potential of failing. Operations on `Buf`
and `BufMut` are infallible.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buf](https://docs.rs/buf/index.html)
- Utilities for working with buffers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)
- A cheaply cloneable and sliceable chunk of contiguous memory.
- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.BytesMut.html)- Mut
- A unique reference to a contiguous slice of memory.
- [TryGet](https://docs.rs/struct.TryGetError.html)- Error
- Error type for the `try_get_`methods of`Buf``Buf``try_get_`methods.

# once_cell - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/^1.9.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, [ unsync::OnceCell](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.OnceCell.html) and

[. A](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.OnceCell.html)

`sync::OnceCell``OnceCell` might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can
be assigned to at most once and provides direct access to the stored
contents. The core API looks *roughly*like this (and there’s much more inside, read on!):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T> OnceCell<T> {
    const fn new() -> OnceCell<T> { ... }
    fn set(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> { ... }
    fn get(&self) -> Option<&T> { ... }
}
```
Note that, like with [ RefCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html) and

[, the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex``set` method requires
only a shared reference. Because of the single assignment restriction `get`
can return a `&T` instead of `Ref<T>` or `MutexGuard<T>`.The `sync` flavor is thread-safe (that is, implements the [ Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Sync.html) trait),
while the

`unsync` one is not.[§](https://docs.rs#recipes)Recipes

`OnceCell` might be useful for a variety of patterns.

[§](https://docs.rs#safe-initialization-of-global-data)Safe Initialization of Global Data

```
use std::{env, io};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Logger {
    // ...
}
static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Logger> = OnceCell::new();
impl Logger {
    pub fn global() -> &'static Logger {
        INSTANCE.get().expect("logger is not initialized")
    }
    fn from_cli(args: env::Args) -> Result<Logger, std::io::Error> {
       // ...
    }
}
fn main() {
    let logger = Logger::from_cli(env::args()).unwrap();
    INSTANCE.set(logger).unwrap();
    // use `Logger::global()` from now on
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazy-initialized-global-data)Lazy Initialized Global Data

This is essentially the `lazy_static!` macro, but without a macro.

```
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
fn global_data() -> &'static Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>> {
    static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = OnceCell::new();
    INSTANCE.get_or_init(|| {
        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
        m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
        Mutex::new(m)
    })
}
```
There are also the [ sync::Lazy](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.Lazy.html) and

[convenience types to streamline this pattern:](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.Lazy.html)

`unsync::Lazy````
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA: Lazy<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = Lazy::new(|| {
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
    m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
    Mutex::new(m)
});
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", GLOBAL_DATA.lock().unwrap());
}
```
Note that the variable that holds `Lazy` is declared as `static`, *not*
`const`. This is important: using `const` instead compiles, but works wrong.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-purpose-lazy-evaluation)General purpose lazy evaluation

Unlike `lazy_static!`, `Lazy` works with local variables.

```
use once_cell::unsync::Lazy;
fn main() {
    let ctx = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let thunk = Lazy::new(|| {
        ctx.iter().sum::<i32>()
    });
    assert_eq!(*thunk, 6);
}
```
If you need a lazy field in a struct, you probably should use `OnceCell`
directly, because that will allow you to access `self` during
initialization.

```
use std::{fs, path::PathBuf};
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
struct Ctx {
    config_path: PathBuf,
    config: OnceCell<String>,
}
impl Ctx {
    pub fn get_config(&self) -> Result<&str, std::io::Error> {
        let cfg = self.config.get_or_try_init(|| {
            fs::read_to_string(&self.config_path)
        })?;
        Ok(cfg.as_str())
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazily-compiled-regex)Lazily Compiled Regex

This is a `regex!` macro which takes a string literal and returns an
*expression* that evaluates to a `&'static Regex`:

```
macro_rules! regex {
    ($re:literal $(,)?) => {{
        static RE: once_cell::sync::OnceCell<regex::Regex> = once_cell::sync::OnceCell::new();
        RE.get_or_init(|| regex::Regex::new($re).unwrap())
    }};
}
```
This macro can be useful to avoid the “compile regex on every loop iteration” problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-include_bytes)Runtime `include_bytes!`

The `include_bytes` macro is useful to include test resources, but it slows
down test compilation a lot. An alternative is to load the resources at
runtime:

```
use std::path::Path;
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct TestResource {
    path: &'static str,
    cell: OnceCell<Vec<u8>>,
}
impl TestResource {
    pub const fn new(path: &'static str) -> TestResource {
        TestResource { path, cell: OnceCell::new() }
    }
    pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        self.cell.get_or_init(|| {
            let dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
            let path = Path::new(dir.as_str()).join(self.path);
            std::fs::read(&path).unwrap_or_else(|_err| {
                panic!("failed to load test resource: {}", path.display())
            })
        }).as_slice()
    }
}
static TEST_IMAGE: TestResource = TestResource::new("test_data/lena.png");
#[test]
fn test_sobel_filter() {
    let rgb: &[u8] = TEST_IMAGE.bytes();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lateinit)`lateinit`

`LateInit` type for delayed initialization. It is reminiscent of Kotlin’s
`lateinit` keyword and allows construction of cyclic data structures:

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct LateInit<T> { cell: OnceCell<T> }
impl<T> LateInit<T> {
    pub fn init(&self, value: T) {
        assert!(self.cell.set(value).is_ok())
    }
}
impl<T> Default for LateInit<T> {
    fn default() -> Self { LateInit { cell: OnceCell::default() } }
}
impl<T> std::ops::Deref for LateInit<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        self.cell.get().unwrap()
    }
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct A<'a> {
    b: LateInit<&'a B<'a>>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct B<'a> {
    a: LateInit<&'a A<'a>>
}
fn build_cycle() {
    let a = A::default();
    let b = B::default();
    a.b.init(&b);
    b.a.init(&a);
    let _a = &a.b.a.b.a;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-std)Comparison with std

| `!Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `Cell<T>` | `T` | requires `T: Copy`for`get` |
| `RefCell<T>` | `RefMut<T>`/`Ref<T>` | may panic at runtime |
| `unsync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once |

| `Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `AtomicT` | `T` | works only with certain `Copy`types |
| `Mutex<T>` | `MutexGuard<T>` | may deadlock at runtime, may block the thread |
| `sync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once, may block the thread |

Technically, calling `get_or_init` will also cause a panic or a deadlock if
it recursively calls itself. However, because the assignment can happen only
once, such cases should be more rare than equivalents with `RefCell` and
`Mutex`.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rustc-version)Minimum Supported `rustc` Version

If only the `std`, `alloc`, or `race` features are enabled, MSRV will be
updated conservatively, supporting at least latest 8 versions of the compiler.
When using other features, like `parking_lot`, MSRV might be updated more
frequently, up to the latest stable. In both cases, increasing MSRV is *not*
considered a semver-breaking change and requires only a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

The implementation is based on the
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/) and

[crates and](https://github.com/indiv0/lazycell/)

`lazy_cell`[. In some sense,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Once.html)

`std::sync::Once``once_cell` just streamlines and unifies
those APIs.To implement a sync flavor of `OnceCell`, this crates uses either a custom
re-implementation of `std::sync::Once` or `parking_lot::Mutex`. This is
controlled by the `parking_lot` feature (disabled by default). Performance
is the same for both cases, but the `parking_lot` based `OnceCell<T>` is
smaller by up to 16 bytes.

This crate uses `unsafe`.

[§](https://docs.rs#faq)F.A.Q.

**Should I use the sync or unsync flavor?**

Because Rust compiler checks thread safety for you, it’s impossible to
accidentally use `unsync` where `sync` is required. So, use `unsync` in
single-threaded code and `sync` in multi-threaded. It’s easy to switch
between the two if code becomes multi-threaded later.

At the moment, `unsync` has an additional benefit that reentrant
initialization causes a panic, which might be easier to debug than a
deadlock.

**Does this crate support async?**

No, but you can use
[ async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell) instead.

**Does this crate support  no_std?**

Yes, but with caveats. `OnceCell` is a synchronization primitive which
*semantically* relies on blocking. `OnceCell` guarantees that at most one
`f` will be called to compute the value. If two threads of execution call
`get_or_init` concurrently, one of them has to wait.

Waiting fundamentally requires OS support. Execution environment needs to
understand who waits on whom to prevent deadlocks due to priority inversion.
You *could* make code to compile by blindly using pure spinlocks, but the
runtime behavior would be subtly wrong.

Given these constraints, `once_cell` provides the following options:

- The `race`module provides similar, but distinct synchronization primitive which is compatible with`no_std`. With`race`, the`f`function can be called multiple times by different threads, but only one thread will win to install the value.
- `critical-section`feature (with a- `-`, not- `_`) uses- `critical_section`to implement blocking.

**Can I bring my own mutex?**

There is [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) to
allow just that.

**Should I use  std::cell::OnceCell, once_cell, or lazy_static?**

If you can use `std` version (your MSRV is at least 1.70, and you don’t need
extra features `once_cell` provides), use `std`. Otherwise, use `once_cell`.
Don’t use `lazy_static`.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related crates

- Most of this crate’s functionality is available in `std`starting with Rust 1.70. See`std::cell::OnceCell`and`std::sync::OnceLock`.
- [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
- [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
- [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
- [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
- [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
- [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
- [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell)(bring your own mutex)

---

# protobuf_support - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf-support/=3.7.2/

## Expand description

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^1.0.30/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`by hand, and switching from handwritten impls to thiserror or vice versa is not a breaking change.
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display`impl is generated for your error if you provide`#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {})", i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From`impl is generated for each variant that contains a`#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()`method is implemented to return whichever field has a`#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()`method is implemented to provide whichever field has a type named`Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace`. Using`Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()`method is forwarded to the source’s`provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and Display methods straight through to an underlying error without adding an additional message. This would be appropriate for enums that need an “anything else” variant.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# protobuf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/protobuf/latest/target-redirect/protobuf/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#library-to-read-and-write-protocol-buffers-data)Library to read and write protocol buffers data

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate has one feature, which is `with-bytes`.

`with-bytes` enables `protobuf` crate support for
[ bytes crate](https://github.com/tokio-rs/bytes):
when parsing bytes or strings from

`bytes::Bytes`,
`protobuf` will be able to reference the input instead of allocating subarrays.Note, codegen also need to be instructed to generate `Bytes` or `Chars` for
`bytes` or `string` protobuf types instead of default `Vec<u8>` or `String`,
just enabling option on this crate is not enough.

See `Customize` struct in [ protobuf-codegen crate](https://docs.rs/protobuf-codegen).

[§](https://docs.rs#accompanying-crates)Accompanying crates

- `protobuf-json-mapping`
- `protobuf-codegen`- `.proto`crates.
- `protoc-bin-vendored`- `protoc`command packed into the crate.
- `protobuf-parse`- `.proto`file parser. Rarely need to be used directly, but can be used for mechanical processing of- `.proto`files.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [descriptor](https://docs.rs/descriptor/index.html)
- Generated file from `google/protobuf/descriptor.proto`
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Utilities to support “extension” fields.
- [plugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/index.html)
- Generated file from `google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.proto`
- [reflect](https://docs.rs/reflect/index.html)
- Reflection implementation for protobuf data
- [rt](https://docs.rs/rt/index.html)
- Functions and types used by generated protobuf code
- [rustproto](https://docs.rs/rustproto/index.html)
- Generated file from `rustproto.proto`
- [text_](https://docs.rs/text_format/index.html)- format
- Protobuf “text format” implementation.
- [well_](https://docs.rs/well_known_types/index.html)- known_ - types
- Generated code for “well known types”

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chars](https://docs.rs/struct.Chars.html)
- Thin wrapper around `Bytes`which guarantees that bytes are valid UTF-8 string. Should be API-compatible to`String`.
- [Coded](https://docs.rs/struct.CodedInputStream.html)- Input - Stream
- Buffered read with handy utilities.
- [Coded](https://docs.rs/struct.CodedOutputStream.html)- Output - Stream
- Buffered write with handy utilities
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumOrUnknown.html)- OrUnknown
- Protobuf enums with possibly unknown values are preserved in this struct.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type for protobuf operations.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageField.html)- Field
- Wrapper around `Option<Box<T>>`, convenient newtype.
- [Special](https://docs.rs/struct.SpecialFields.html)- Fields
- Special fields included in each generated message.
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/struct.UnknownFields.html)- Fields
- Hold “unknown” fields in parsed message.
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/struct.UnknownFieldsIter.html)- Fields - Iter
- Iterator over `UnknownFields`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/enum.UnknownValue.html)- Value
- Unknown value.
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/enum.UnknownValueRef.html)- Value - Ref
- Reference to unknown value.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [VERSION](https://docs.rs/constant.VERSION.html)
- protobuf crate version
- [VERSION_](https://docs.rs/constant.VERSION_3_7_2.html)- 3_ - 7_ - 2
- This symbol can be referenced to assert that proper version of crate is used

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.Enum.html)
- Trait implemented by all protobuf enum types.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.EnumFull.html)- Full
- Trait is implemented for all enum types if lite runtime is not requested.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.Message.html)
- Trait which is implemented by all generated message.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.MessageDyn.html)- Dyn
- Dynamic-dispatch version of either generated message or dynamic message.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.MessageFull.html)- Full
- Trait implemented for all the generated messages, except when lite runtime is enabled.
- [Oneof](https://docs.rs/trait.Oneof.html)
- Trait implemented by all oneof types in generated code.
- [Oneof](https://docs.rs/trait.OneofFull.html)- Full
- Implemented by all oneof types when lite runtime is not enabled.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# protobuf_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf-codegen

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#protobuf-code-generator-for-protobuf-crate)Protobuf code generator for `protobuf` crate

This crate is useful mostly from `build.rs` scripts to generate `.rs` files during the build.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-generate-code)How to generate code

There are three main ways to generate `.rs` files from `.proto` files:

- using `protoc`command line tool and`protoc-gen-rs`plugin
- using this crate `Codegen`with pure rust parser
- using this crate `Codegen`with`protoc`parser

Which one should you use depends on your needs.

If you are using non-cargo build system (like Bazel), you might prefer
using `protoc-gen-rs` plugin for `protoc`.

If you build with `cargo`, you probably want to use `Codegen` from this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#protoc-parser-vs-pure-rust-parser)Protoc parser vs pure rust parser

There are two protobuf parsers which can be plugged into this crate:

- `protoc`-based parser (- `protoc`is a command like utility from Google protobuf)
- pure rust parser (`protobuf-parse`crate)

`protoc`-based parser is expected to parse `.proto` files very correctly:
all Google’s protobuf implementations rely on it.

While there are no known bugs in `protobuf-parse`, it is not tested very well.
Also `protobuf-parse` does not implement certain rarely used features of `.proto` parser,
mostly complex message options specified in `.proto` files.
I never saw anyone using them, but you have been warned.

Note `protoc` command can be obtained from
[ protoc-bin-vendored](https://docs.rs/protoc-bin-vendored) crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Use this in build.rs
protobuf_codegen::Codegen::new()
    // Use `protoc` parser, optional.
    .protoc()
    // Use `protoc-bin-vendored` bundled protoc command, optional.
    .protoc_path(&protoc_bin_vendored::protoc_bin_path().unwrap())
    // All inputs and imports from the inputs must reside in `includes` directories.
    .includes(&["src/protos"])
    // Inputs must reside in some of include paths.
    .input("src/protos/apple.proto")
    .input("src/protos/banana.proto")
    // Specify output directory relative to Cargo output directory.
    .cargo_out_dir("protos")
    .run_from_script();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-protoc-gen-rs)How to use `protoc-gen-rs`

If you have to.

(Note `protoc` can be invoked programmatically with
[protoc crate](https://docs.rs/protoc/))

- Install protobuf for `protoc`binary.

On OS X [Homebrew](https://github.com/Homebrew/brew) can be used:

`brew install protobuf`On Ubuntu, `protobuf-compiler` package can be installed:

`apt-get install protobuf-compiler`Protobuf is needed only for code generation, `rust-protobuf` runtime
does not use C++ protobuf library.

- Install `protoc-gen-rs`program (which is`protoc`plugin)

It can be installed either from source or with `cargo install protobuf-codegen` command.

- Add `protoc-gen-rs`to $PATH

If you installed it with cargo, it should be

`PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"`- Generate .rs files:

`protoc --rs_out . foo.proto`This will generate .rs files in current directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#customize-generate-code)Customize generate code

Sometimes generated code need to be adjusted, e. g. to have custom derives.

rust-protobuf provides two options to do that:

- generated `.rs`files contain`@@protoc_insertion_point(...)`markers (similar markers inserts Google’s protobuf generator for C++ or Java). Simple script`sed`one-liners can be used to replace these markers with custom annotations.
- `Codegen::customize_callback`can be used to patch generated code when invoked from- `build.rs`script.

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

rust-protobuf since version 3 no longer directly supports serde.

Rust-protobuf 3 fully supports:

- runtime reflection
- JSON parsing and printing via
`protobuf-json-mapping`

Which covers the most of serde use cases.

If you still need serde, generic customization callback (see above) can be used
to insert `#[serde(...)]` annotations.

[Example project](https://github.com/stepancheg/rust-protobuf/tree/master/protobuf-examples/customize-serde)
in the rust-protobuf repository demonstrates how to do it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Codegen](https://docs.rs/struct.Codegen.html)
- Entry point for `.proto`to`.rs`code generation.
- [Customize](https://docs.rs/struct.Customize.html)
- Specifies style of generated code.
Generated files can be customized using this proto
or using `rustproto.proto`options.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Customize](https://docs.rs/trait.CustomizeCallback.html)- Callback
- Dynamic callback to customize code generation.

---

# protobuf_parse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf-parse

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#parse-proto-files)Parse `.proto` files

Parse `.proto` file definitions, **not** the protobuf text format serialization.

Files can be parsed using pure Rust parser (mod `pure`)
or using the `protoc` command (mod `protoc`).

This crate is not meant to be used directly, but rather through the `protobuf-codegen` crate.
If you think this crate might be useful to you,
please [consider creating an issue](https://github.com/stepancheg/rust-protobuf/issues/new),
until that this crate is considered to have **no stable API**.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [pure](https://docs.rs/pure/index.html)
- Pure rust `.proto`file parser.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Configure and invoke `.proto`parser.
- [Proto](https://docs.rs/struct.ProtoPath.html)- Path
- Protobuf file relative normalized file path.
- [Proto](https://docs.rs/struct.ProtoPathBuf.html)- Path - Buf
- Protobuf file relative normalized file path.

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/0.4.7/num_bigint/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::ONE;
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the [/](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. Their serialized data is generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- [Random](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomBits.html)- Bits - `rand`
- A random distribution for `BigUint``BigInt`
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- The error type returned when a checked conversion regarding big integer fails.
- [U32Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U32Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u32`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [U64Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U64Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u64`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigUint.html)- BigUint - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigUint`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Rand](https://docs.rs/trait.RandBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- A trait for sampling random big integers.
- [ToBig](https://docs.rs/trait.ToBigInt.html)- Int
- A generic trait for converting a value to a `BigInt``None`when converting from`f32`or`f64`, and will always succeed when converting from any integer or unsigned primitive, or`BigUint`
- [ToBig](https://docs.rs/trait.ToBigUint.html)- Uint
- A generic trait for converting a value to a `BigUint`

# rite_stdlib - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-stdlib/0.3.1/rite_stdlib/

## Expand description

Standard action library for Rite ceremonies.

This crate provides the built-in action implementations:

- **Verification**:- `clock_check`,- `confirm`,- `check_value`,- `oral_readback`,- `machine_info`
- **Attestation**:- `attest`
- **Crypto**:- `generate_keypair`,- `export_public`,- `wrap_key`,- `unwrap_key`
- **PKI**:- `generate_csr`,- `issue_certificate`

[§](https://docs.rs#backend-integration)Backend integration

All crypto and PKI actions require a backend; there are no software
fallbacks. For dry-run mode, configure a `MockBackend` in your
ceremony YAML.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `verification`: verification actions (requires- `subtle`,- `sysinfo`)
- `attestation`: attestation recording
- `crypto`: crypto actions (- `generate_keypair`,- `export_public`,- `wrap_key`,- `unwrap_key`)
- `pki`: PKI actions (- `generate_csr`,- `issue_certificate`; requires- `x509-cert`,- `der`,- `sha1`,- `rsa`,- `p256`)
- `default`: all features enabled

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use rite_stdlib::default_registry;
let registry = default_registry();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [MockBackend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.MockBackend.html);

- `pub use pki::`- [GenerateCsrAction](https://docs.rs/pki/struct.GenerateCsrAction.html);

# rite_render - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-render/0.3.1/rite_render/

## Expand description

Document generation for Rite ceremonies.

- `script`: printable HTML briefing produced from a resolved- `rite_model::Ceremony`- `rite script`).
- `report`: post-ceremony HTML report produced from a verified- `StepFact`transcript (consumed by- `rite report`).

Rendering uses embedded [minijinja](https://docs.rs/minijinja) templates with a built-in theme
selected via [ Theme](https://docs.rs/enum.Theme.html), and optional run-time

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Branding.html)

`Branding`[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

- [path_](https://docs.rs/path_resolver/index.html)- resolver
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Runtime schema generation traits for GTS types.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_cast/index.html)- cast
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_compat/index.html)- compat
- OP#12 – Schema-vs-schema compatibility validation.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_modifiers/index.html)- modifiers
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_narrow/index.html)- narrow
- Typed narrowing — go from a runtime-typed payload (commonly
`serde_json::Value`) to a typed GTS view`Q: GtsSchema`, validating the runtime schema-id discriminator against the target’s`<Q as GtsSchema>::innermost_type_id()`and deserialising the payload into`Q`via [`crate::GtsDeserializeWrapper`].
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_refs/index.html)- refs
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_resolver/index.html)- resolver
- `$ref`resolution for registered GTS schemas: inlining- `gts://`and local- `#/`references into a self-contained body. A- `$ref`target is inlined at a non-root position, so its root-only keys (- `$id`/- `$schema`and the- `x-gts-*`type-level modifiers) are stripped on the way in.- `allOf`and the other combinators are preserved verbatim — composition is left to the JSON Schema validator, not flattened here.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_traits/index.html)- traits
- OP#13 – Schema Traits Validation (`x-gts-traits-schema`/`x-gts-traits`)
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- [x_](https://docs.rs/x_gts_ref/index.html)- gts_ - ref

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [gts_](https://docs.rs/macro.gts_schema_for.html)- schema_ - for
- Generate a GTS-style schema for a nested type with allOf and $ref to base.

# rite_openssl - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-openssl/0.3.1/rite_openssl/

## Expand description

OpenSSL backend for Rite ceremonies.

Provides [ OpenSslBackend](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenSslBackend.html), a software cryptographic backend backed by OpenSSL.
Keys are held in memory for the lifetime of the backend instance.

[§](https://docs.rs#capabilities)Capabilities

[ OpenSslBackend](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenSslBackend.html) implements the following

[traits:](https://docs.rs/rite-sdk/0.3.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rite_sdk/index.html)

`rite_sdk`- `KeyStoreBackend`
- `SignBackend`
- `KeyTransportBackend`
- `RandomBackend`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

- `vendored`: bundle OpenSSL at build time (no system library needed). Required for air-gapped USB image builds.

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenSslBackend.html)- SslBackend
- OpenSSL-based cryptographic backend.

# rite_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-runtime/0.3.1/rite_runtime/

## Expand description

Execution runtime for Rite ceremonies.

`rite-runtime` defines the protocol that frontends use to drive a
ceremony to completion, the executor that walks the ceremony plan,
and the supporting machinery for transcripts and action handlers.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-types)Key types

- `Executor`
- `Action`- `ActionRegistry`
- `BackendRegistry`- `BackendFactory`
- `Reporter`
- `TranscriptSink`

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_support/index.html)- support
- Test-only helpers for action implementors.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DERIVATION_](https://docs.rs/constant.DERIVATION_V1.html)- V1
- Frozen-scheme tag recorded with the machine seed. It pins the *entire*construction (Extract/Expand, the ratchet rule, the`info`/path byte encodings), not merely the hash. A verifier treats it as a selector among known-good schemes it already trusts and rejects any value it does not recognise, it is never an instruction to trust an arbitrary algorithm.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_DRAW_LEN.html)- DRAW_ - LEN
- Longest value a single draw can produce: the `HKDF-Expand`output limit of`255 * HashLen`bytes (RFC 5869), with SHA-256’s 32-byte output. [`expand`] panics beyond this, so anything replaying a recorded draw must bound the requested length by this value first.

- Source of wall-clock time for a ceremony run.
- [Transcript](https://docs.rs/trait.TranscriptSink.html)- Sink
- Synchronous, durable observer of `StepFact`

- Build a derivation path. The single place the path format lives, so the
draw side and the verify side cannot drift. A `purpose`is drawn at most once per step, so`(epoch, step, purpose)`uniquely identifies a value.

- Evaluate an `ExprValue`to a string.

- Advance the ratchet by one epoch, folding in a human contribution.

- Compute `seed_0`from the machine entropy`m`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_params.html)- params
- Deserialize the per-step parameter blob into a typed handler-specific struct.

# harn_dap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-dap/0.8.168/harn_dap/

## Expand description

Harn debug adapter (DAP).

Exposed as a library so the single multi-call `harn` binary can dispatch
into the debug adapter when launched under the `harn-dap` name (see
`harn-cli`’s `main`), instead of shipping a second fully-linked binary.
The thin `src/main.rs` shim keeps `harn-dap` buildable as its own binary.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Run the Harn debug adapter over stdio until the client disconnects.

# harn_guard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-guard/0.8.168/harn_guard/

## Expand description

`harn-guard` — the downloadable on-device prompt-injection classifier for
Harn (security Layer 2).

This crate is the **management layer**: a catalog of upstream, already-hosted
models ([ catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)), an on-disk store that installs and verifies them
(

[), and selector resolution (](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)

`store`[). It hosts nothing, bundles no weights, and makes no network calls itself — the CLI downloads from the catalog’s upstream URLs on the user’s machine and hands the bytes to](https://docs.rs/resolve/fn.resolve_dir.html)

`resolve_dir`[for SHA-256 verification + atomic install.](https://docs.rs/store/struct.GuardStore.html#method.install)

`GuardStore::install`The heavy inference runtime (ONNX) lives behind the off-by-default `neural`
feature, so the default binary never links a model runtime. When built
without it, [ load_classifier](https://docs.rs/fn.load_classifier.html) is a no-op returning

`None` and the runtime
keeps using the always-available built-in heuristic classifier. When built
with it, a host installs [into the runtime’s lazy loader seam (](https://docs.rs/fn.load_classifier.html)

`load_classifier``harn_vm::security::set_injection_classifier_loader`), which fires the
first time a `local-ml` policy scores untrusted content.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# rite_resolver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-resolver/0.3.1/rite_resolver/

## Expand description

Ceremony resolver: parse YAML, validate, and produce IR.

This crate transforms ceremony YAML into the [ rite_model::Ceremony](https://docs.rs/rite-model/0.3.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rite_model/ir/ceremony/struct.Ceremony.html) IR
ready for execution. It owns the YAML schema (AST types), the lowering
pipeline, and the resolution pass.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use rite_resolver::resolve;
let ceremony_yaml = r#"
version: "0.2"
name: "Example Ceremony"
roles: {}
sections: {}
"#;
// Resolve from a string (no execution-time inputs).
let result = resolve(ceremony_yaml, None);
assert!(result.is_ok(), "ceremony should resolve: {:?}", result.errors);
```
For a file with rich, span-anchored diagnostics, use [ analyze](https://docs.rs/fn.analyze.html); for a
ceremony plus its included files, use

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_files.html)

`resolve_files`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ceremony](https://docs.rs/struct.CeremonyInputs.html)- Inputs
- External inputs collected from CLI flags (`--param`,`--role`,`--material`) and environment variables (`RITE_PARAM_*`,`RITE_ROLE_*`,`RITE_MATERIAL_*`).
- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.Diagnostic.html)
- A diagnostic message with optional source location.
- [Reference](https://docs.rs/struct.ReferenceEntry.html)- Entry
- A single reference site collected during span walking.
- [Resolve](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolveResult.html)- Result
- Result of resolution, containing either a value or accumulated errors.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A source location within a YAML file (1-indexed line and column).
- [SpanMap](https://docs.rs/struct.SpanMap.html)
- Maps ceremony element IDs to their source positions for diagnostic enrichment and editor navigation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Reference](https://docs.rs/enum.ReferenceContext.html)- Context
- The container (step or section) that owns a reference site.
- [Reference](https://docs.rs/enum.ReferenceTarget.html)- Target
- The kind of declaration a reference points to.
- [Resolve](https://docs.rs/enum.ResolveError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur during ceremony resolution.
- [Resolve](https://docs.rs/enum.ResolveWarning.html)- Warning
- Warnings that don’t prevent resolution but may indicate issues.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Severity of a diagnostic.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [analyze](https://docs.rs/fn.analyze.html)
- Parse and validate a ceremony file, returning both the resolved ceremony and diagnostics.
- [analyze_](https://docs.rs/fn.analyze_str.html)- str
- Parse and validate ceremony YAML from an in-memory string.
- [resolve](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve.html)
- Parse and resolve a ceremony from a YAML string.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_files.html)- files
- Parse and resolve a ceremony from a file path.

# rite_model - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-model/0.3.1/rite_model/

## Expand description

Core domain model and IR for the Rite ceremony DSL.

`rite-model` defines the Intermediate Representation (IR): the fully resolved
ceremony data consumed by the executor. The YAML schema (parser input) lives in
`rite-resolver`; this crate contains only the runtime-facing types.

[§](https://docs.rs#module-structure)Module structure

- `ir`- `Ceremony`- `Step`- `Role`
- `expression`- `${artifact.name | sha256 | hex}`syntax
- `transcript`- `StepFact`+ friends)
- `safe_path`
- `types`(private): Shared semantic enums:- `ActionType`- `DutyType`

[§](https://docs.rs#backendconfig)`BackendConfig`

Re-exported from `rite-sdk` for convenience. The canonical definition lives there.

# sandogasa_sourcehut - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-sourcehut/0.15.3/sandogasa_sourcehut/

## Expand description

GraphQL client for the Sourcehut (sr.ht) API.

Unlike the GitHub-ish forges, sr.ht has no unified PR model and splits
activity across independent services, each exposing its own GraphQL
endpoint at `https://<service>.<host>/query`. This crate covers the
surface `sandogasa-report` needs to summarize a contributor’s activity:

- **lists.sr.ht**—- `Client::patches`
- **todo.sr.ht**—- `Client::ticket_events`
- **git.sr.ht**—- `Client::repositories`- `Client::commits_since`- `Client::user_email`

Conventions (see `DEVELOPMENT.md`): requests are `POST {query, variables}` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (a personal access
token from meta.sr.ht/oauth2/personal-token, which by default grants
all scopes). Cursored resolvers return `{results, cursor}`; pass the
cursor back until it is null. Timestamps are RFC3339 UTC, which sort
lexicographically — so string comparison is a valid date comparison.

The `host` is passed in full (`sr.ht`, or a self-hosted host), so the
client works against any deployment.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Actor](https://docs.rs/struct.Actor.html)
- An entity (user/mailbox) reference, identified by its canonical name
(`~username`for a registered sr.ht user).
- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- A sr.ht GraphQL client bound to one instance host.
- [Commit](https://docs.rs/struct.Commit.html)
- A git commit from a repository log.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)
- One ticket-activity event from the authenticated user’s todo.sr.ht
feed. An event bundles one or more `EventDetail`
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventDetail.html)- Detail
- One change within an `Event``event_type`tags which kind it is (`CREATED`,`STATUS_CHANGE`, …); the actor/status fields are populated only for the matching kind (via GraphQL inline fragments).
- [Named](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedRef.html)- Ref
- A `{ name }`reference (mailing list, repository, …).
- [Patchset](https://docs.rs/struct.Patchset.html)
- A patchset submitted to a mailing list (lists.sr.ht).
- [Repo](https://docs.rs/struct.Repo.html)
- A git.sr.ht repository (only the name is needed to drive the log).
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)
- A git author/committer signature.
- [Ticket](https://docs.rs/struct.TicketRef.html)- Ref
- The ticket an `Event`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_token.html)- token
- Check whether `token`is accepted by the instance, via`{ me { username } }`on git.. `Ok(true)`for a valid token,`Ok(false)`for a rejected one (401 or a GraphQL error),`Err`if the server can’t be reached — so callers can tell “rejected” from “unreachable”.

---

# protobuf 3.7.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/protobuf/3.7.2

# Library to read and write protocol buffers data

## Features

This crate has one feature, which is `with-bytes`.

`with-bytes` enables `protobuf` crate support for
[ bytes crate](https://github.com/tokio-rs/bytes):
when parsing bytes or strings from

`bytes::Bytes`,
`protobuf` will be able to reference the input instead of allocating subarrays.Note, codegen also need to be instructed to generate `Bytes` or `Chars` for
`bytes` or `string` protobuf types instead of default `Vec<u8>` or `String`,
just enabling option on this crate is not enough.

See `Customize` struct in [ protobuf-codegen crate](https://docs.rs/protobuf-codegen).

## Accompanying crates

- `protobuf-json-mapping`
- `protobuf-codegen`- `.proto`crates.
- `protoc-bin-vendored`- `protoc`command packed into the crate.
- `protobuf-parse`- `.proto`file parser. Rarely need to be used directly, but can be used for mechanical processing of- `.proto`files.

---

                Rust implementation of Google protocol buffers

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf/3.7.2/src/protobuf/lib.rs.html

# protobuf/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Library to read and write protocol buffers data
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! ## Features
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! This crate has one feature, which is `with-bytes`.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! `with-bytes` enables `protobuf` crate support for
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! [`bytes` crate](https://github.com/tokio-rs/bytes):
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! when parsing bytes or strings from `bytes::Bytes`,
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! `protobuf` will be able to reference the input instead of allocating subarrays.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! Note, codegen also need to be instructed to generate `Bytes` or `Chars` for
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! `bytes` or `string` protobuf types instead of default `Vec<u8>` or `String`,
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! just enabling option on this crate is not enough.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! See `Customize` struct in [`protobuf-codegen` crate](https://docs.rs/protobuf-codegen).
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! ## Accompanying crates
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! * [`protobuf-json-mapping`](https://docs.rs/protobuf-json-mapping)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!   implements JSON parsing and serialization for protobuf messages.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! * [`protobuf-codegen`](https://docs.rs/protobuf-codegen)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   can be used to generate rust code from `.proto` crates.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! * [`protoc-bin-vendored`](https://docs.rs/protoc-bin-vendored)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!   contains `protoc` command packed into the crate.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! * [`protobuf-parse`](https://docs.rs/protobuf-parse) contains
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   `.proto` file parser. Rarely need to be used directly,
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!   but can be used for mechanical processing of `.proto` files.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)#![deny(missing_docs)]
[31](https://docs.rs#31)#![deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links)]
[32](https://docs.rs#32)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Descriptor](https://docs.rs/struct.DescriptorProto.html)- Proto
- Describes a message type.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumDescriptorProto.html)- Descriptor - Proto
- Describes an enum type.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumOptions.html)- Options
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumValueDescriptorProto.html)- Value - Descriptor - Proto
- Describes a value within an enum.

- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldDescriptorProto.html)- Descriptor - Proto
- Describes a field within a message.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldOptions.html)- Options
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileDescriptorProto.html)- Descriptor - Proto
- Describes a complete .proto file.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileDescriptorSet.html)- Descriptor - Set
- The protocol compiler can output a FileDescriptorSet containing the .proto files it parses.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileOptions.html)- Options
- [Generated](https://docs.rs/struct.GeneratedCodeInfo.html)- Code - Info
- Describes the relationship between generated code and its original source file. A GeneratedCodeInfo message is associated with only one generated source file, but may contain references to different source .proto files.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageOptions.html)- Options
- [Method](https://docs.rs/struct.MethodDescriptorProto.html)- Descriptor - Proto
- Describes a method of a service.

- Describes a service.
- [Service](https://docs.rs/struct.ServiceOptions.html)- Options
- [Source](https://docs.rs/struct.SourceCodeInfo.html)- Code - Info
- Encapsulates information about the original source file from which a FileDescriptorProto was generated.
- [Uninterpreted](https://docs.rs/struct.UninterpretedOption.html)- Option
- A message representing a option the parser does not recognize. This only appears in options protos created by the compiler::Parser class. DescriptorPool resolves these when building Descriptor objects. Therefore, options protos in descriptor objects (e.g. returned by Descriptor::options(), or produced by Descriptor::CopyTo()) will never have UninterpretedOptions in them.

# protobuf::ext - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf/3.7.2/protobuf/ext/index.html

## Expand description

Utilities to support “extension” fields.

This is a stopgap implementation, it only allows to fetch basic singular values, and that’s it. Anything similar to extension registry is not implemented yet.

Extensions are [described in the official protobuf documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#extensions).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ExtField](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtFieldOptional.html)- Optional
- Optional ext field
- [ExtField](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtFieldRepeated.html)- Repeated
- Repeated ext field

---

# protobuf::reflect - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf/3.7.2/protobuf/reflect/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#reflection-implementation-for-protobuf-data)Reflection implementation for protobuf data

[§](https://docs.rs#generated-vs-dynamic)Generated vs dynamic

rust-protobuf supports reflection for both:

- generated messages (generated rust code)
- dynamic messages (created from arbitrary `FileDescriptorProto`without code generation)

The API to work with these types of messages is the same.

[§](https://docs.rs#api)API

The API roughly follows Google protobuf C++ and Java API. Some minor adjustements are made to make code more idiomatic to rust.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Dynamic representation of enum type.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.EnumValueDescriptor.html)- Value - Descriptor
- Description for enum variant.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Field descriptor.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Reflection for objects defined in `.proto`file (messages, enums, etc).
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Dynamic representation of message type.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageRef.html)- Ref
- Wrapper around either `MessageFull`
- [Method](https://docs.rs/struct.MethodDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Service method descriptor.
- [Oneof](https://docs.rs/struct.OneofDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Oneof descriptor.
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectEqMode.html)- EqMode
- Parameter for `ReflectEq`
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectMapMut.html)- MapMut
- Dynamic mutable reference to `map`field
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectMapRef.html)- MapRef
- Dynamic reference to `map`field
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectOptionalRef.html)- Optional - Ref
- Singular field field and value type.
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectRepeatedMut.html)- Repeated - Mut
- Dynamic mutable reference to repeated field
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectRepeatedRef.html)- Repeated - Ref
- Dynamic reference to repeated field
- [Service](https://docs.rs/struct.ServiceDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Dynamic representation of service type.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/enum.ReflectFieldRef.html)- Field - Ref
- Reference to a value stored in a field, optional, repeated or map.
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/enum.ReflectValueBox.html)- Value - Box
- Owner value of any elementary type
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/enum.ReflectValueRef.html)- Value - Ref
- A reference to a value
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/enum.RuntimeFieldType.html)- Field - Type
- Reflective representation of field type.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/enum.RuntimeType.html)- Type
- Runtime representation of elementary protobuf type.
- [Syntax](https://docs.rs/enum.Syntax.html)
- `.proto`file syntax.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Protobuf](https://docs.rs/trait.ProtobufValue.html)- Value
- Type implemented by all protobuf singular types (primitives, string, messages, enums).
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/trait.ReflectEq.html)- Eq
- Special version of eq.

# protobuf::rt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf/3.7.2/protobuf/rt/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#functions-and-types-used-by-generated-protobuf-code)Functions and types used by generated protobuf code

These are not considered to be public API of rust-protobuf, so they can be changed any time (provided compatibility with previously generated code is preserved).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cached](https://docs.rs/struct.CachedSize.html)- Size
- Cached size field used in generated code.
- [Lazy](https://docs.rs/struct.Lazy.html)

# protobuf::text_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/protobuf/3.7.2/protobuf/text_format/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#protobuf-text-format-implementation)Protobuf “text format” implementation.

Text format message look like this:

```
size: 17
color: "red"
children {
    size: 18
    color: "blue"
}
children {
    size: 19
    color: "green"
}
```
This format is not specified, but it is implemented by all official
protobuf implementations, including `protoc` command which can decode
and encode messages using text format.

[§](https://docs.rs#json)JSON

rust-protobuf also supports JSON printing and parsing.
It is implemented in
[ protobuf-json-mapping crate](https://docs.rs/protobuf-json-mapping/%3E=3.0.0-alpha).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseError.html)- Error
- Text format parse error.

- Parse text format message.
